# Week 2, Day 1.1 — TypeScript check-in: nothing new today

Day 1.2's Playwright code — filling fields, checking boxes, picking from dropdowns — uses
only TypeScript you already have. This lesson is a pointer, not a primer.

> **This day introduces no new TypeScript**, so there is no primer to work through. Go
> straight to [Day 1.2](/learn/w2/d1/p2).

| | |
|---|---|
| **New syntax today** | none — this tab is a 60-second check that last week stuck |
| **Leans on** | [async and the page fixture](/learn/w1/d5/p1) · [chaining onto a locator](/learn/w1/d4/p2) |
| **Then go to** | [Day 1.2](/learn/w2/d1/p2), which is all Playwright API |

## What today's code leans on

| Concept | Status | Where it was taught |
|---|---|---|
| `async` functions, arrow functions | already covered | [Week 1, Day 5.1](/learn/w1/d5/p1) |
| `page` fixture, per-test isolation (preview) | already covered | [Week 1, Day 5.1](/learn/w1/d5/p1) |
| Chaining a method onto a locator | already covered | [Week 1, Day 4.2](/learn/w1/d4/p2) |

Nothing below is new syntax — [Day 1.2](/learn/w2/d1/p2) spends its time on the Playwright
API (`.fill()`, `.check()`, `.selectOption()`), not the language.
Every test today is written `async ({ page }) => { ... }`. What is that `page`?

options: A fresh browser tab, created for this test alone
One shared browser tab that every test in the file takes turns using
The page object for the site under test, which you define yourself
checkpoint.explanation: Each test gets its own `page` — a fresh tab, so nothing one test does leaks into the next. That per-test isolation was [Week 1, Day 5.1](/learn/w1/d5/p1), and Day 5 of this week is about what happens when you split a test and lose it.

blocks.text: No new TypeScript today. If the table above had any surprises in it, follow the link before starting [Day 1.2](/learn/w2/d1/p2) — the Playwright will be easier to see if the language underneath it is not also new.

## What's next

[Day 1.2 — From recorder to real code](/learn/w2/d1/p2) puts these actions to work on a real form.

blocks.text:
# Week 2, Day 1.2 — From recorder to real code: actions on a form

By the end of this lesson you will have hand-written the locators for a full
registration form — text fields, a radio button, checkboxes, a dropdown, and a country
picker — and filled and submitted it without Codegen recording a single line.

| | |
|---|---|
| **You'll use** | `.fill()` · `.pressSequentially()` · `.check()` · `.selectOption()` |
| **On** | [the Register.html signup form](https://demo.automationtesting.in/Register.html) — every control type on one page |
| **Assumes** | [locators](/learn/w1/d4/p2) · [async and the page fixture](/learn/w1/d5/p1) |
| **Not yet** | assertions — nothing here checks the form *worked*. That is [Day 2](/learn/w2/d2/p2). |
> **Try it here.** Write code in the editor on the right and press Run. Your code drives a real browser, and the results appear beside it.

## Two things you already know

- **Codegen only records actions.** [Week 1, Day 4.2](/learn/w1/d4/p2) used it to
  generate locators — it never records an assertion, because it has no way to know what
  you *expect* to happen. [Week 1, Day 5.2](/learn/w1/d5/p2) showed a recorded test
  passing with a wrong password for exactly that reason. Today still has no assertions —
  [Day 2](/learn/w2/d2/p2) adds them.
- Every test is an `async` function, and `page` is a fresh browser tab per test — see
  [Week 1, Day 5.1](/learn/w1/d5/p1) if that's fuzzy. Nothing new there today.

## Today's app

[demo.automationtesting.in/Register.html](https://demo.automationtesting.in/Register.html)
— a real signup form with every control type on one page: text inputs, radios,
checkboxes, a dropdown, and a country picker. No login, no session — every example below
starts fresh on this page.

## Filling text: `.fill()` vs `.type()`

| | `.fill()` | `.type()` (alias `pressSequentially()`) |
|---|---|---|
| How | sets the value directly | simulates one keystroke at a time |
| Speed | fast | slower — real per-key delay |
| Default choice | **yes** | only when the page reacts to each keystroke (autocomplete, a keyup handler) |

Measured on this page, filling the same 24-character string: `.fill()` **68ms**,
`.type()` **92ms**. The gap widens with longer text and more fields — use `.fill()` unless
you have a specific reason not to.

| Line | What it does |
|---|---|
| `getByPlaceholder("First Name")` / `("Last Name")` | placeholder text is unique for each — verified, 1 match apiece |
| `page.locator("textarea")` | Address has no placeholder or label — it's the only `<textarea>` on the page, so the tag alone is enough |
| `input[type='email']` / `input[type='tel']` | no label text on either field, so the `type` attribute is the next-best identifier |

**Expected result:** the screenshot shows all five fields filled.

**Challenge:** swap `.fill()` for `.pressSequentially()` on one field, with `{ delay: 50 }`, and watch it type letter by letter.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.
blocks.starter:
const { browser, page } = await launch();
await page.goto("https://demo.automationtesting.in/Register.html");

variation.prompt: Same five fields, different data: fill the form for a learner of your own invention. Then switch ONE of the five to `.pressSequentially()` with `{ delay: 50 }` and watch that field type itself out letter by letter while the other four snap in at once.

blocks.text:
## Radio buttons and checkboxes — `.check()`

Both use the same method. Playwright clicks whatever is needed to make the box or radio
end up checked — you never compute whether it already is.

| Line | What it does |
|---|---|
| `input[value='FeMale']` | no `id` on the radios, so matched by the `value` attribute — verified: 1 match |
| `#checkbox1` / `#checkbox2` | verified ids; map to Cricket and Movies respectively |

**Expected result:** the FeMale radio and both checkboxes show checked in the screenshot.

**Challenge:** call `.check()` again on the same checkbox and confirm nothing breaks — `.check()` is idempotent.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.
blocks.starter:
const { browser, page } = await launch();
await page.goto("https://demo.automationtesting.in/Register.html");

variation.prompt: Same two methods, different controls: check the other gender radio, reading its `value` off the page rather than guessing the spelling, and add the Hockey checkbox alongside Cricket. The lesson only verified the ids for Cricket and Movies, so Hockey's is yours to find.

blocks.text:
## Dropdowns — `.selectOption()`

Pick by the **visible text** a user would read, or the underlying `value` where the two
match — either way, verify the option actually exists first.

| Line | What it does |
|---|---|
| `#Skills` `.selectOption({ label: "Java" })` | matches by visible text; verified 78 options, single-select despite the name |
| `#country` `.selectOption("India")` | matches by the option's `value`, which equals its text here; verified 11 real countries |

**Expected result:** screenshot shows "Java" selected in Skills and "India" in the country picker.

**Gotcha, verified:** `#country` carries `aria-hidden="true"` and a Select2 CSS class
(`select2-hidden-accessible`) — on many Select2 widgets that blocks `.selectOption()` and
forces you to click a fake dropdown instead. On this app it does not block it; `.selectOption()`
works directly. Always verify a skinned `<select>` for real rather than assuming either way.

**Challenge:** try `.selectOption("Select Country")` on `#countries` and read the timeout — that select genuinely has no other option to find.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.
blocks.starter:
const { browser, page } = await launch();
await page.goto("https://demo.automationtesting.in/Register.html");

variation.prompt: Same method, different picks: select a skill other than Java by its label, and a country other than India. Then point `.selectOption()` at `#countries`, the dead `Country*` field, and read the timeout it gives you before it gives up.

blocks.text:
## Doing it for real, in a spec file

Same actions, written to a real `.spec.ts` and run with `npx playwright test`. No
`expect()` yet — that's the whole point. This test cannot currently tell you whether any
of it actually worked, only that nothing threw. [Week 1, Day 5.2](/learn/w1/d5/p2)
showed the same gap with a wrong password; [Day 2](/learn/w2/d2/p2) closes it.

> ▶ **Run it yourself.** `npx playwright test week2/generated/day1-register-form.spec.ts`
>
> It passes — but "passes" here only means nothing threw. Nothing in the file checks that
> the form actually accepted the data. Closing that gap is [Day 2](/learn/w2/d2/p2).

## Best practices

- Default to `.fill()`; reach for `.pressSequentially()` only when the page reacts per keystroke.
- `.selectOption({ label })` when the visible text is what a tester would read; a plain string when value and label match.
- Never assume a Select2-skinned `<select>` is off-limits to `.selectOption()` — verify it.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | What you see | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Selecting the "Country*" field (`#countries`) | timeout — it has one dead option | use `#country` instead |
| Assuming "Select Skills" is multi-select | only the last `.selectOption()` call sticks | it's a single-select — verified, no `multiple` attribute |
| Typing "Female" | 0 matches | the page really does spell it `FeMale` |
You are filling a search box that shows autocomplete suggestions as you type, and the suggestions are what you need to click. Which method fills it?

options: `.fill()` — it is the default, and faster
`.pressSequentially()`, because the page reacts to each keystroke
Either — they produce identical events, only at different speeds
checkpoint.explanation: `.fill()` sets the value directly, so a page listening for per-key events never hears them and the suggestions never appear. That is exactly the case the lesson reserves `.pressSequentially()` for — it costs you the speed (68ms vs 92ms measured here) and you spend it deliberately.

blocks.text: On `#Skills` you call `.selectOption({ label: "Java" })`, then `.selectOption({ label: "Python" })`. What is selected at the end?

options: Both Java and Python — it has 78 options and takes multiple
Java only — the first pick wins and later calls are ignored
Neither — the second call throws, because the option is already taken
checkpoint.explanation: "Select Skills" reads like a multi-select and has 78 options, but it carries no `multiple` attribute — verified in the lesson. A single-select keeps only your last pick, so Python replaces Java silently. Nothing errors, which is what makes it worth knowing.

blocks.text: The spec at the end of this lesson reports `1 passed`. What has it actually proved?

options: That the form accepted the data and the registration succeeded
That every locator matched and no line threw — nothing more
That the page navigated away after Submit
checkpoint.explanation: There is not one `expect()` in that file, so "passed" means only that nothing threw on the way through. It is the same gap [Week 1, Day 5.2](/learn/w1/d5/p2) showed with a wrong password, and [Day 2](/learn/w2/d2/p2) is where you close it.

blocks.text:
- `.fill()` by default. `.pressSequentially()` only when the page reacts to each keystroke.
- `.check()` makes a control checked — it does not toggle it, so calling it twice is safe and you never compute the current state first.
- `.selectOption({ label })` matches the visible text; a bare string matches the option's `value`.
- Verify a skinned `<select>` rather than assuming. `#country` carries `aria-hidden` and a Select2 class and still takes `.selectOption()` — on another app it might not.
- **A test with no `expect()` cannot fail for the right reason.** Everything today is actions; assertions start tomorrow.

## What's next

[Day 1.3](/learn/w2/d1/p3) takes this exact code and shows how a real project would organize it.

parts.title: The same actions, the way a real project writes them

blocks.text:
# Week 2, Day 1.3 — The same actions, the way a real project writes them

By the end of this lesson you will have pulled yesterday's fill/check/select steps out
of one test and into a single reusable function two different tests both call.

> **No new API here on purpose.** Everything below is something you already ran in
> [Day 1.2](/learn/w2/d1/p2). The only new thing is the structure around it.

| | |
|---|---|
| **New API** | none — every line here is something you ran in [Day 1.2](/learn/w2/d1/p2) |
| **What changes** | where the code lives: ten repeated lines become one `fillRegistrationForm(page, email)` |
| **Not yet** | the Page Object Model. This is a plain function; the class version is week 3. |

## The problem with what we wrote yesterday

Every test that needs a filled-out registration form has to repeat the same ten lines —
`.fill()`, `.check()`, `.selectOption()`, one after another. Two tests means those ten
lines exist twice; a real suite might need them in thirty places. If the form gets a new
required field, that is thirty edits, not one.

## Same code, with structure around it

| In Day 1.2 you wrote | Here it becomes | Why |
|---|---|---|
| ten `.fill()`/`.check()`/`.selectOption()` lines inline in the test | one call: `await fillRegistrationForm(page, email)` | the steps live in one place — change the form once, not in every test |
| a hardcoded email string | a parameter | the one thing tests actually need to vary is pulled out; everything else stays fixed |

**This is a function, not a class.** Grouping locators and actions into a class — the
Page Object Model — is coming formally in week 3. Today's version reaches for the
simplest tool that already solves the repetition: a function.

### Why it is shaped this way

| Choice | Reason |
|---|---|
| `page: Page`, `email: string` typed parameters | the function is explicit about what it needs and returns — same typing rules as any other function |
| Exported into its own file, not the spec | reusable from every spec that needs this form, not just one |
| No `expect()` inside it | this function performs actions — a preview of the "no assertions in a page object" rule week 3 names formally. Nothing to assert yet, since Day 1 doesn't check outcomes at all |

**Expected result:** `2 passed`. Both tests call the same function with a different email —
the ten-line form-filling sequence exists exactly once in the whole project.

## What a reviewer would look for

- The repeated steps live in one function, not copy-pasted across tests.
- The function is named for what it does (`fillRegistrationForm`), not for the DOM calls inside it.
- Nothing inside it asserts anything.
The helper is saved as `registration-helpers.ts`, deliberately not `registration-helpers.spec.ts`. Why does the suffix matter?

options: The runner collects every `*.spec.ts` file and would try to execute a file with no tests in it
TypeScript refuses to export a function from a `.spec.ts` file
It is only a naming convention — either name works identically
checkpoint.explanation: The spec suffix is what the runner globs for. A helper that carries it gets collected and executed as a test file, and a file with no `test()` calls in it is an error, not a pass. The rule gets named formally in week 3.

blocks.text: Why does `fillRegistrationForm` take `email` as a parameter, but keep the first name, address and phone hardcoded?

options: Because strings are the only type a helper can safely accept
Because the email is the one value these tests actually need to differ — parameterising the rest would add knobs nobody turns
Because Playwright requires every helper to take exactly one parameter beyond `page`
checkpoint.explanation: Two tests register two learners, and the only thing that has to differ between them is the email. Everything else is fixed on purpose. Problem 3 asks you to add the phone as a second parameter — because there the tests do need it to vary.

blocks.text:
- Repetition across tests is a structural problem, not a typing problem: ten lines in thirty specs is thirty edits when the form changes.
- The fix is the simplest thing that works — a function. The Page Object Model is the same instinct with a class around it, and it arrives in week 3.
- Name a helper for what it does (`fillRegistrationForm`), not for the calls inside it.
- No `expect()` inside a helper that performs actions. That is a preview of the "no assertions in a page object" rule, and it holds for the same reason.

## What's next

[Day 1.4](/learn/w2/d1/p4) — your turn, with no worked examples to lean on.

# Week 2, Day 1.4 — Practice: actions on a form

Three problems, getting harder. No answer key — you learn this by getting it wrong and
reading the error message.

Write spec files into `week2/generated/` and run them with `npx playwright test`.

> Struggling for more than about twenty minutes on one problem means the gap is in
> [Day 1.2](/learn/w2/d1/p2) or [Day 1.3](/learn/w2/d1/p3), not in your ability. Go back, re-read, come here again.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Three problems** | Beginner → Advanced, no answer key on the first two |
| **Pulls on** | [Day 1.2](/learn/w2/d1/p2) for the actions · [Day 1.3](/learn/w2/d1/p3) for the structure |
| **If you stall** | more than ~20 minutes on one means the gap is in the lesson, not in you — go back and re-read |

## When you are done

Re-read your Problem 3 function and ask what Day 1.3 was really about: if this form
grew a required "State" field tomorrow, how many files would you have to touch?

problems.statement:
**What to build.** Fill in the First Name, Last Name, Address, Email, and Phone fields
on the Register.html form with your own made-up values.

**Where.** A cell in this lesson, using `launch()` and `show()`.

**How you will know it worked.** The screenshot shows every field filled in, and none of the five locators throws.

> **Hint** — every field but the two you already know needs the `type` attribute or the tag name.

**What to build.** A QA lead wants every registration to always pick the **FeMale**
radio and the **Hockey** checkbox, plus two skills and a country of your choice, then
submit.

**Where.** A cell here, or a spec in `week2/generated/` if you want to run it for real.

**How you will know it worked.** A screenshot right before `#submitbtn` is clicked shows
all of it selected — radio, checkbox, both skills, country.

**What to build.** Extend [Day 1.3](/learn/w2/d1/p3)'s `fillRegistrationForm` — add a
second parameter for the phone number instead of the hardcoded one — then write a spec
in `week2/generated/` that calls it twice with two different email/phone pairs.

**Where.** Edit `week2/generated/registration-helpers.ts` directly, then a spec in `week2/generated/`.

**How you will know it worked.** `npx playwright test` on your new spec reports `2 passed`, and the function signature now takes both values as parameters instead of one.
